speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under the common law, the injured employee has to initiate legal actions and prove his employer's negligence to succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The WICA provides a cheaper and quicker alternative for an injured employee to claim work injury compensation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under WICA, the employee does not need to prove the employer's fault or negligence in order to be compensated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: He will be compensated as long as the injury happened in the course of work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is why we say WICA is a no-fault regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In exchange, the employer's amount of compensation is capped under WICA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: All claimants, except five on average per year, were compensated by the deadline set by the Ministry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The common reason for non-payment was because the employer was uninsured and faced financial difficulties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In such situations, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) will assist the injured employees using the Workers' Fund.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: WICA has served its role of compensating injured workers well, but can be improved further, in four main ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, the aims of MOM's work injury compensation regime should not be confined to compensation after injury has happened.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: It should also incentivise employers to prevent injuries from happening in the first place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Our Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) 2028 aspiration for Singapore is to be amongst the best in the world in WSH standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Second, some WICA claims still take too long before payout is made.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will speed up and improve claims processing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Third, we will enhance insurance coverage and benefits for injured workers and employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In the recommendations of the WSH2028 Tripartite Strategies Committee in April this year, they were convinced that the key in preventing injuries is in aligning the commercial interests of employers and insurers closer to preventing injuries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In short, we need to make WSH good for businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: More companies will then be self-motivated to prevent injuries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: One of the features in the new WICA is designed to influence employers to be more proactive on prevention by making the business impact of injuries more significant, through its effect on premiums.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Information transparency on claims history is essential in influencing employers to be safer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, there is no information sharing among insurers of their clients' past claims records.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This has resulted in safer companies subsidising the less safe companies as there is little premium differentiation between these companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The WSH2028 Tripartite Strategies Committee recommended that MOM facilitate the sharing of WICA claims data with insurers to sharpen the premium differentiation between safer and less safe companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The relevant data will be made available to all designated insurers approved by the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Furthermore, to facilitate more accurate premium pricing, all designated insurers will be able to verify their clients' declared aggregated workforce size and annual payroll through MOM's database.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Clients' actual workforce size and payroll data will remain confidential and will not be disclosed to insurers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: What the insurers will know is whether their clients' declarations are consistent or not consistent with MOM's records, within a certain margin of error.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: With greater information transparency, employers with good safety records should be able to enjoy lower premiums.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: More importantly, less safe employers who are faced with higher premiums will have greater commercial incentive to put in place measures to prevent their employees from getting injured in the first place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Next, we have proposed five amendments which aim to speed up and improve WIC claims processing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, we will designate insurers to provide WIC insurance under clause 31.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These designated insurers will be required to process insured WIC claims in accordance with clauses 36, 44 to 47.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, insurers only process WIC claims for temporary incapacity (TI).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For fatal and permanent incapacity (PI), these claims are processed by the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In contrast, insurers are already processing the claims for all other types of insurance, such as life, medical and travel insurance, in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Other jurisdictions that also adopt the private WIC insurance model, such as certain states in the United States (US) and Australia, have also required WIC insurers to process all insured claims.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Allowing insurers to process WIC claims can help to speed up claims processing as insurers, who are the payers, do not need to do duplicative work to verify the documents and evidence obtained by MOM on the claim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To ensure that the interests of all parties will continue to be protected under this new process, the Ministry will put in place a system of checks and balances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Clauses 31 to 34 allow the Commissioner to impose licensing conditions on designated WIC insurers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The Commissioner may conduct third party audits on insurers to make sure that they comply with the Commissioner’s conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Any insurer that fails to comply with the Commissioner's conditions may be subject to administrative financial penalties or, in more serious cases, have their WIC designation suspended or revoked.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under an insurer-processing regime, employees' and employers' interests will continue to be protected in four key ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: First, insurers have to comply with the Commissioner's protocol on claims admissibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The grounds for liability for compensation under the new Bill remain the same as that in the existing Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will set out guidelines to ensure that insurers do not reject claims which are currently admissible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Third, in terms of processing, insurers have to meet the processing timelines set by the Commissioner to ensure that the injured employees continue to receive their compensation promptly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Objections will continue to be adjudicated by the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Another recommendation to speed up claims processing is to allow compensation to be based on the prevailing state of incapacity that is unlikely to change significantly after the date of assessment of the incapacity, termed "current incapacity" or CI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The remaining 20% take longer to resolve due to the time required for a PI assessment to be made.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The PI percentage is one of the factors determining the amount of lump-sum compensation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, delay in settling the compensation means injured employees will receive their compensation later, employers of injured foreign employees will incur higher upkeep and maintenance expenses, as well as increased uncertainty for all parties involved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have consulted the WIC medical board members who advised that the extent of incapacity at six months after accident is a close approximation of the eventual state of the PI in most cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Clause 15 of the Bill and the First Schedule to the Bill allow lump-sum compensation to be computed based on the CI assessment that is made at least six months after the date of accident.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will help to expedite claims payout to the employee or their families for many long-drawn claims.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The default expectation is for CI to be assessed as soon as possible after six months from the accident.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Nonetheless, doctors will still have the professional discretion to assess for PI at a later date if they believe that the extent of incapacity will change further for more complex injuries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Another cause of delay is disputes over AME.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Such disputes may delay claims processing up to one and a half months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Currently, the Commissioner uses documentary evidence, such as pay slips, to compute the employee's AME for purposes of WICA compensation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: If the employee's pay slip is not available, the Commissioner can compute compensation based on a co-worker's pay slip.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, there are cases where there is no documentary evidence of the employee's or the co-workers' pay slip.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Therefore, the First Schedule to the Bill will also empower the Commissioner to compute the employee's earnings based on a multiple of the employee's basic rate of pay, called the derived AME, if there is no other reliable evidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The derived AME will be set at the higher end of industry norm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is to ensure that employees are not disadvantaged due to the absence of reliable evidence to compute the actual AME.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We also propose to streamline the claim process to provide for more hassle-free "auto-claim" for fatal and serious injuries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Currently, an employee or his representative needs to submit a WICA claim application for fatal or PI compensation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Insurers or the Commissioner will start to process the claims once there is a notice of accident, without the employee needing to submit a separate claims application.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under this regime, employees who do not wish to make a claim under WICA can still opt out at a later stage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Delays can be also caused by parties not cooperating with the Commissioner or the designated insurers in the claims process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To avoid such delays, we will make it an offence under clause 50 for parties who fail to comply with the Commissioner's direction to provide information or documents to the designated insurer or the Commissioner necessary for claims processing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: If accidents do happen, we are also enhancing the protection and benefits for injured employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under current WICA, employers are required to compensate all their injured employees, regardless of their salaries, where they work, and the nature of work, manual or non-manual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To help employers fulfil this obligation, employers are required to purchase insurance for all manual employees and non-manual employees (NMEs) working in factories earning up to $1,600 a month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The Minister will amend the WICA subsidiary legislation to align with the salary threshold for non-workmen under Part IV of the Employment Act to give added protection to these employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will be done in phases to allow employers time to adjust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In Phase 2, we will further increase the monthly salary threshold to $2,600 a month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Nonetheless, we do not expect significant cost impact to businesses as MOM's Conditions of Employment survey indicates that close to 90% of employees are already covered by WICA insurance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Even though employers were not obligated to cover some of them, but employees are covered 90% today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: By doing so, these companies ensure that they could meet their WICA obligations in case of an accident.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The First Schedule to the Bill extends compensation to employees on light duties due to work injuries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will put them on par with employees on medical leave due to work injuries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: An employee injured at work could be given medical leave or light duties, depending on his fitness to work and availability of light duties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Employers would benefit from an employee who is fit enough to carry out light duties, as there would be shorter downtime from work and some restoration of productive capacity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, an employee on light duties may be earning less than his usual salary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is because he is likely to work at a lower intensity and duration and will miss out on overtime pay or allowances that he would normally have received if he was not injured.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The First Schedule requires employers to compensate the difference between what the employee earns on light duties, and his AME, which is what he normally earns, including overtime, bonuses and allowances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Compensation is payable only if the employee's actual wages, while he was on light duties, are less than what he would have received as his AME compensation under WICA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is to ensure that an employee who is on light duties due to a work injury is not worse off than an injured employee on medical leave, because the one on medical leave would have been given compensation of AME.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In addition, the WICA subsidiary legislation will require employers to report any instance of employees on medical leave or light duties due to a work injury.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is to address the concern that some irresponsible employers may try to avoid reporting work accidents by attempting to influence doctors to give fewer days of medical leave or light duties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will simplify the reporting requirements for accidents with less than four days of medical leave or light duties to minimise the administrative burden on companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, an injured employee's PI assessment is typically done by a doctor directed by the employer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, MOM has received feedback, one from Member Louis Ng as well, that some errant employers may attempt to influence doctors to give inadequate medical leave or some doctors may be overly conservative and underestimate the percentage of PI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To ensure there is proper and fair assessment of the extent of work injury sustained by the employee, clause 37 of the Bill which requires an employee to attend medical examination required by the employer, has an exception which enables the Commissioner to allow employees to undergo medical examination by another doctor doing the PI assessment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This would be exercised, for example, if there are concerns and prima facie evidence that the quality of care and incapacity assessment by the employer's doctor may not be adequate or fair.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: MOM will also update the WICA compensation limits in the First Schedule to the Bill to keep pace with wage growth and healthcare costs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is a regular update which we do once every four years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: It prevents the real value of compensation from being eroded by inflation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is to account for the growth in median gross monthly income since the last review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will ensure that the limit for medical expenses continues to cover more than 95% of all WICA claims medical expenses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: While we work to make the WIC framework better for employees, it is equally important to ensure that the interests of the employers are also protected.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Employers who buy insurance policies that do not adequately cover their WICA liabilities may not be able to obtain reimbursement for compensation paid.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have come across cases where construction companies bought WICA policies that do not cover accidents arising from working above a certain height, and certain activities, such as digging and piling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: But these are precisely the type of work where accidents are more likely to happen.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: To better safeguard employers' interests when buying WIC insurance policies, clause 26 of the Bill allows the Commissioner to prescribe a core set of standard terms for WICA-compliant policies to ensure that insurance policies cover employers' WICA liabilities adequately.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will also make insurers accountable for the policies they offer to employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Clause 26 of the Bill requires any insurer who has sold to the employer a policy purporting to be a WICA-compliant policy, to compensate the injured employee according to the standard terms of a WICA-compliant policy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is on top of it being an offence under clause 30 for insurers to sell policies purporting to be WICA-compliant when they are not.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under the current WICA, the Commissioner can order the employee to refund the employer any medical leave wages paid if the employee withdraws his claim, if the accident was subsequently determined not to be work-related, or if it was a false claim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will extend the refund to lump-sum compensation and medical expenses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Clauses 16 and 54 of the Bill enable the Commissioner to order the claimant to refund the employer or insurer, if the employer or insurer had paid for the lump-sum compensation or medical expenses due to error or false or misleading information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This is on top of it being an offence under clause 62 for any person to obtain compensation by providing false or misleading information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Under the current Act, parties have up to 14 days from the receipt of the notice of assessment to raise objections to the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: If no objection is raised within the 14-day timeline, the notice of assessment takes the effect of an order of compensation, and such orders cannot be appealed to the High Court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will amend the Act to allow late objections with valid reasons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: MOM had come across a case where the employee had given the completed objection form to the employer to submit to the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: However, the employer failed to submit the employee's objection form within the prescribed 14-day timeline due to administrative lapses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: While the employer had appealed for the Commissioner to accept the late objection, current WICA does not allow for late objections irrespective of the reasons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Therefore, we have provided in clauses 46 and 49 of the Bill to allow the Commissioner to accept late objections if the late objection is due to error or fraud by another person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In addition, we will create a new offence under the same clause for failure to deposit compensation with the Commissioner when directed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Both offences are benchmarked to non- or delayed payment of salary under the Employment Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will make WICA better for both employers and employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have worked with the tripartite partners and other key stakeholders to design the new WIC Bill to support our WSH2028 vision.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: With these changes and all other ongoing and upcoming efforts under the WSH2028 strategy, and continued strong support from our tripartite partners, we endeavour to reduce workplace accidents and raise Singapore's WSH standards to be amongst the best in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will give sufficient lead time for the industry to adjust to the changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The WIC framework is a no-fault system with the aim of providing workers injured in work-related accidents with low-cost and expeditious means to claim WIC.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Bill seeks to improve the framework to better enable the meeting of its objectives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Briefly, the amendments to the Bill are commendable in the following areas.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is beneficial in the sense that there is less incentive for employers to influence doctors to prescribe fewer days of MC to the injured workers, to circumvent the original reporting requirement of only needing to report injuries which result in death, or at least MCs of four days.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will ensure that both employers and employees' interests are better protected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For employees, there is more certainty in receiving compensation, especially if employers face financial difficulty.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As for the employers, they would know with greater certainty that they would be reimbursed under the insurance policies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is a recognition on the Government's end of the financial implications that workplace injuries have on people, such as loss of income and hefty medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, insurers will now be required to share policy and claims information with MOM and such data will be centralised and available to other insurers, too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With this information, insurers are better placed to price the premiums based on their risk profile and claims history.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Companies with fewer work injuries will enjoy lower premiums, compared to less safe ones.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this aspect, companies will be incentivised to ensure a safe work environment for their workers, which is likewise beneficial for them, as healthy and happy workers will be more productive and efficient at work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the other hand, workers benefit when they return home safely.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As this group of junior PMEs are within the lower salary range, the compulsory additional coverage will provide greater assurance both financially and emotionally of coverage in the event of work injuries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As for companies, while at first it appears that it is an increased financial outlay in terms of insurance premiums, it must be borne in mind that, should there be work injuries, the insurers will step in, which is a cost-saving measure in the long run.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Where companies observe safety measures at work, there is the potential for lower insurance premiums.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the changes proposed under the Bill are welcomed, I would like to suggest some further enhancements to the proposed changes aimed at expediting the WIC claims process and expanding the scope of mandatory insurance coverage.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Under the Bill, all work injuries resulting in any instance of light duty or medical leave would have to be reported by the employer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To speed up the claims process, WIC claims will be processed for all work injuries reported by the employer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will overcome the problem where the worker is not aware that he or she had to file the WIC claim and is subsequently time-barred from doing so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Licensed insurers will process all claims arising from accredited WIC policies to reduce the number of disputes arising from policies with complex exclusions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Last year, following a stepping up of enforcement efforts by MOM, 39 employers were fined for failing to report work injuries, compared to only one employer in 2017.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I note that under this Bill, the penalty imposed on employers for failing to report work injuries has been increased.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Auto-processing of WIC claims would only serve the injured worker if employers comply with their work injury reporting obligations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I would suggest the following measures to be taken to support the amendments proposed under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, MOM should audit employers to ensure that employers are complying with their obligations to report work injuries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This could be done with reference to third-party data, such as information from workers, unions and medical practitioners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Accurate reporting of workplace injuries will provide a true representation of the extent of workplace accidents in Singapore and provide important information to licensed insurers to enable them to assess the premiums payable by the company.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Apart from implementing audits on the employers to ensure compliance on their part, perhaps more could be done to educate workers and their respective union leaders of their employers' reporting obligations under the law, lest they be fearful of adverse repercussions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For instance, conducting seminars for the union leaders or workers, or stating such avenues or measures in the Employee Handbook which workers and employees can access on the employers' obligations to report work injuries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is hoped that with more transparency accorded in the process, there will be a decline in failures to report work injuries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, injured workers should be kept in the loop in the WIC claim process so that they are able to access the documentation trail and make informed decisions concerning the claim, such as whether to elect to take the claim to Court instead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Injured workers should be notified when the employer reports the work injury and be kept abreast of developments in the WIC claim process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If for some reason, the worker elects to pursue his claim in Court, it is likely that the employer may not be pleased with such a move for various reasons, such as bad publicity, legal costs and so on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Perhaps it needs to be reiterated and emphasised that during the course of the litigation process the employer is not allowed to terminate the employee for reasons associated with the accident, save where permitted by law, failing which there might be legal consequences.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, while the WIC claim is being processed, the employer should ensure that the injured worker is able to seek the medical attention that he or she requires in an expedient manner with the employer's support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There have been reported incidences where injured workers were not able to seek medical treatment because the employer did not provide them with a Letter of Guarantee and the workers had to go without treatment as they were unable to afford medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, there must be avenues for injured workers to raise issues encountered in the WIC claims process to MOM.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There have been past incidences where vulnerable workers have been coerced by employers to conceal work injuries in order to remain in employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some errant employers have also terminated employment arrangements of injured foreign workers and sent the workers home to escape liability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the introduction of lower premiums for "safer" companies, some companies may be incentivised to under report work injuries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As such, there must be avenues for workers or whistleblowers to report any malpractice for MOM's investigation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is odd that the workers are not able to be paid the full AME for as long as they are on light duties, especially if the sole reason for being placed on light duties is because of their work injuries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Perhaps, it is time to explore the possibility of paying the workers the full AME for the full period that they are placed on light duties and not limit it to the first 14 days.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Granted that this could possibly mean increased costs on the employer' side while not being able to reap the full economic benefits from the employees and workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, it should be borne in mind that the decision and/or duration for light duties is ultimately the doctors' decision, and based on a true and accurate assessment of the workers' sustained injuries and the doctors' assessment on how long the worker requires to fully recuperate before being fully fit to perform his original duties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In any case, any increased costs on the employers' part should be reimbursed by the WIC insurance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Additionally, the Government should also work with unions to continue encouraging companies which employ professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) earning more than S$2,600 to also buy insurance for peace of mind of employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, it is important to bear in mind that the costs of insurance premiums would pale in comparison with the amount a company without insurance may have to pay an employee who suffers work injury under the common law.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In any case, given that the risk profile of NMEs is significantly lower than manual employees, insurance premiums for NMEs would be lower.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers can work with unions and the Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC) for their foreign-worker workforce to raise workers' awareness of their rights under the WIC framework.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This will reduce the worker's anxiety in the event a work injury is sustained and smoothen the work injury complaint process for all parties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Unions or MWC, as the case may be, can also assist workers with their queries on the WIC claim process to enable them to make informed choices concerning the WIC claim.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Workers can also seek free legal advice through the legal clinics offered by the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and MWC, in partnership with the Law Society of Singapore's Pro Bono Services Office.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There have been instances where some errant employers have terminated insurance coverage for their foreign workers within the term of their Work Pass or had overlooked renewal of coverage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Previously known as Workmen's Compensation, the concept of providing compensation against workplace injuries via legislative fiat dates back to the late 19th century.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore today, manual workers are covered regardless of salary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: R was employed as an Industrial Relations Officer by a union.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He was injured when he was on his way to attend a labour workshop some years ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the time of the accident, he did not make a claim under WICA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His employer informed him that they would take care of the medical costs arising out of the accident.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The employer did the needful and incurred medical expenses which included a surgical procedure that saw four screws inserted into R's spine.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: R returned to work after his hospitalisation leave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As he approached the age of 67 a few years after the accident, he was informed by his superiors that his employment would not be extended.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The matter of his injury came up just before he left the employ of the union.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His injuries had left him unable to find another employer who would hire him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And separately, in need of medical follow-up, R then decided to make a belated WICA claim to MOM.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was originally rejected due to it being out of time and because, in the Commissioner of Labour's assessment, the accident he was involved in did not arise out of and in the course of his employment and, hence, rejected for the purposes of a WICA claim.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This position was, in fact, wrong in law, but this initial conclusion by the Commissioner of Labour could have turned on how R framed the circumstances of his injury.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An appeal was thereafter made to the Commissioner of Labour which was successful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Where useful, I will refer to R's case in raising them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first set of queries are general in nature.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the outset, a question that comes to mind in R's case is why he did not file a claim independent of his employer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I put the question to R to which he replied that the matter did not cross his mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: R could have been under the mistaken belief that since the accident occurred outside his usual place of work, it was not claimable under WICA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But even if R was labouring under that presumption, his employer should have known better, which then begs the question why the employer did not proceed in making a WICA claim for him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I am not aware if R falls under the category of those who chose private compensation, it is a relevant question whether the support or compensation received from employers is adequate in all of these 2,500-odd cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, does MOM follow up with employers and make the necessary enquiries with regard to private settlements and workers' decisions not to proceed with claims so that workers are not worse off than they would be under the WICA framework?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If MOM does so, how do cases like R's slip through the cracks?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More specifically, would MOM monitor private settlements between employers and workers under the amended Bill and would MOM consider a more activist approach in overseeing private settlements to ensure that workers get a fair deal?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A power relationship exists, one that can be incredibly lopsided, regardless of whether local or foreign workers are involved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Very often, discussions over workers' rights can gloss over this lived reality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some may wish not to make trouble for their bosses for the fear of being ostracised or labelled or even sent home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet, some others may fear for their jobs and simply bottle things up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Other more specific issues for specific groups of workers can also come up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2017, in a TODAY article, Transient Workers Count Too (TWC2), a well-known non-governmental organisation (NGO) reported that some lawyers pursue questionable practices with regard to foreign workers who are ill-informed about electing between a WICA claim on the one hand and common law remedy on the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, the Archdiocesan Commission for the Pastoral Care of Migrants and Itinerant People said foreign workers are sometimes "poorly informed about costs" involved in legal processes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, one of the main purposes of the Bill, that is, to provide for a more expeditious process for workers to receive compensation for injuries suffered arising out of and in the course of employment is to be welcomed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 1975, when this Bill's predecessor, the Workmen's Compensation Bill came up for Second Reading, the intention to introduce an expeditious compensation regime was a key purpose of the law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In those days, in the words of then Manpower Minister Ong Pang Boon, some employers even ignored the notice of assessment and, despite repeated reminders, would even delay the payment of compensation by disputing the extent of liability to pay compensation or the extent of the dependency of the claimants on the earnings of a deceased worker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But as this House has heard in the past, most recently when the Act was amended in 2011, the reality is that workers need enough information to assess how best to pursue their injury claims as not all are highly educated and informed or know of their rights and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What R's experience suggests is that in spite of the various initiatives to make workers aware of their rights, much more can be done, and the modified claims framework that underpins the changes proposed under this Bill is a good opportunity to review how WICA is communicated to all workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Coming back this Bill, in view of the fact that most of the feedback on the public consultation to it came from insurers, I would like to ask the Minister how MOM will ensure that all employers adhere to the new WICA processing regime.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2008, MOM committed itself to raising worker awareness of avenues for compensation through the community, union leaders and employers so as to create awareness among employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does MOM plan to engage employers and workers to further improve compliance to the new claims reporting framework and to better protect workers' rights after the passage of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a fundamental change in the claims framework and it requires a religious compliance commitment from employers to make it work smoothly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2017, the Minister of State for Manpower in a reply to a Parliamentary Question confirmed that it was mandatory and not voluntary for employers to report any work-related accidents resulting in an employee's death or hospitalisation for at least 24 hours, or medical leave for more than three days.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that regard, the Minister of State stated that MOM had taken enforcement action against errant employers for persistent late reporting of minor injuries after repeated reminders or delayed reporting of a serious work injury, with seven employers taken to task.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Are they issued warning letters, stern warnings or reminders in the first instance?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that the regime is escalatory and calibrated to deal with egregious employers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm this to be the case and, if so, how many warnings has MOM issued to employers over the last five years, from reminders to warnings, amongst others, and finally, prosecutions?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And in the case of R, what action would MOM typically take against an employer in his scenario under the new amendments?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, over the last five years, I would like to enquire how many WICA claims were outside the one-year claims window and how many of these were successful claims.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is probable that R would receive a similar response from an insurer in the first instance, that of being out of time, under the new claims regime proposed under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 36 of the Bill gives the Commissioner broad powers to process a claim.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of this, what new roles, if any, will MOM or the Commissioner of Labour play to support the claims process for workers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, would MOM consider all appeals that fall outside the claims window to be addressed by the Commissioner of Labour at the first instance, so that the workers can deal directly with the regulator for advice and assistance?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would give effect to the Commissioner of Labour's powers to override an insurer's assessment under the amended Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, such a work process would support its objective of making the claims process as worker-friendly as possible and position the Ministry as a proactive intermediary for all WICA claims.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share a broadly exhaustive list of the circumstances under which the Commissioner of Labour will take over the processing of a WICA claim as opposed to insurers leading the process as envisaged under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The proposal was agreed to by the then Minister for Manpower.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Since then, I understand the Ministry has decided that WICA compensation limits will be reviewed once every four years instead.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the Minister explain why this is the case and consider reverting to the three-year review window to give workers a higher payout, particularly those struck by permanent and debilitating injuries?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister would agree that even though the new limits may not differ significantly from one year to another, a few thousand dollars can make an important difference for workers or their families.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, it raised clause 37 and medical examinations that a worker must surrender himself or herself to if injured in the line of work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A reality of Singapore's workforce is that much of the manual work is carried out by foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the last few years, we have read about doctors falling far below the standards of their profession, ostensibly because they are beholden to a worker's employer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is mind-boggling to wrap one's conscience around some of the headlines and the stories that have appeared in the local mainstream media on this matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A doctor wrote to the Straits Times Forum page, in response to the story, to state that doctors cannot be site inspectors to verify if a company is in a position to extend the appropriate light duties to a worker, as the reality may be that the employer has no light duties it can reasonably offer the injured worker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An important condition could be that the consultation fees and medical costs are within a stipulated range so as not to disadvantage the employer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such ongoing scrutiny and prospective improvements will ensure our manpower laws are effective, fit for purpose and protect our workforce.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand from the handout that the Minister of State has shared that workers can go to another doctor if they are not satisfied with the initial diagnosis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the new WICA claims processing regime comes into being, I hope the Ministry not only puts the welfare of the worker first but puts itself in the shoes of our workers and their lived reality, as it operationalises the amendments to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have made great strides in prioritising WSH.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our WSH2028 strategy articulates a Vision Zero for all stakeholders to work towards preventing all forms of injury and ill-health at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While we work towards the WSH2028 vision, the work injury compensation regime provides a safeguard for employees who, unfortunately, have suffered a workplace injury.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this distressing period, work injury compensation helps to alleviate some of the financial burden on employees and to ensure that they have access to the necessary medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have the following clarifications and recommendations on how the proposed amendments will be implemented in Subsidiary Legislation and operational policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The problem of some doctors giving insufficient medical leave to migrant workers has been a recurring problem for several years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the first case, Dr Kevin Yip gave two days of medical leave and light duties thereafter to Mr Zhang, a construction worker, despite the latter having a serious fall that resulted in multiple injuries, such as a fractured collarbone and a few rib fractures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the second case, Dr Wong Him Choon likewise gave two days of medical leave and light duties thereafter to Mr Fan, also a construction worker, despite the latter sustaining hand and forearm fractures that required surgery after a fall from height.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Errant employers may influence medical practitioners to prescribe lesser days of medical leave and provide light duties in order to downplay the severity of an injury or to avoid reporting the accident.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I previously asked the Ministry whether the requirement for reporting work-related or workplace accidents can include cases where the employee is placed on light duties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the reporting requirements for a workplace accident will be updated in Subsidiary Legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will help address cases of doctors under-prescribing medical leave to employees so that employers can avoid reporting an accident.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, my concern is that doctors may now circumvent this requirement by not prescribing any medical leave or light duties at all.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has stated that the Singapore Medical Council (SMC) has mechanisms to take disciplinary action against doctors who do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this requires a process of detection, investigation and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The employee who has suffered a work injury may be denied access to medical documentation, proper and timely medical treatment and compensation in the meantime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Ministry monitor incidences of medical malpractices by doctors under the new reporting requirements?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, will the Ministry consider implementing a dual reporting system by both doctors and employers in the future?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is welcome as it is now very common for injured employees to be prescribed light duties in lieu of medical leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I understand that there is a lot of confusion on the ground as to what constitutes light duties and when an injured employee can be prescribed light duties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The SMC Ethical Code and Guidelines require doctors to ensure that there are appropriate light duties available to the employee at their workplaces before prescribing light duties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In practice, I understand that many doctors prescribe light duties when, in fact, there are no light duties available at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This leads to confusion for both the employees and the employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are stories of employees who end up not working at all or employees who do heavy labour that is inappropriate for their physical conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that this is an issue that will have to involve the Ministry of Health, SMC and doctors and return-to-work occupational therapists.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that light duties are now more significant under the work injury compensation regime, will the Ministry work with the relevant stakeholders to shed more light on what constitutes light duties and when it can be prescribed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the Ministry has also stated that employees will receive notice of accident reports after they have been submitted to the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The accident report and claim application state important details, such as the location of the accident, the nature of the injury, and the AME.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are key details that will affect the compensation assessment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MOM confirm that the employee will receive notice of the accident report and claim application in all cases?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the employee be given the opportunity to challenge the details stated in the accident report and claim application where they are filed by the employer or automatically processed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can MOM share how it intends to ensure that the accident report and claim application will reach the hands of a migrant worker whose address is likely to be the office address of their employer?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the accident report and claim application be sent to the migrant worker through existing mobile applications?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Alternatively, do employees have the right to obtain copies of these documents directly from MOM free of charge?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the Bill proposes for licensed insurers to process insured WICA claims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this move will help to expedite the claims process and ensure timely payouts for employees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two points relating to processing of claims by insurers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that injured employees are sometimes caught in limbo where their employer has not paid for medical treatment and refuses to provide a Letter of Guarantee for the necessary medical procedures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Requiring that employees hold insurance cards not only benefits them, it will also take some of the burden off employers and reduce the amount of bad debt hospitals face due to unpaid medical bills by employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that MOM can issue a letter to help migrant workers open a Post Office Savings Bank (POSB) payroll account at the Kaki Bukit branch.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The feedback from non-governmental organisations (NGOs) is that this is a good practice, and some have suggested to me that we institutionalise this practice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will also be of great assistance to insurers who can make more easily their payouts through bank transfers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, as insurers will now take over the processing of claims, the task of determining AME now falls on them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that determining the AME can be a contentious issue and there are incidences of erroneous, missing and forged timecards and salary slips.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a difficult enough problem for MOM with their statutory powers of investigation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Where a dispute over the AME goes to the Commissioner, the Bill empowers the Commissioner to compute compensation based on a multiple of the employee’s basic monthly salary if there are no other evidence available.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if it will issue guidelines for determining what this multiple should be or if the issue is left entirely up to the discretion of the Commissioner?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, employers are currently required to provide adequate food and acceptable housing for migrant workers during the entire injury compensation process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is not clear what adequate food and acceptable housing means.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NGOs have shared with me horror stories where migrant workers are required to travel long distances to their work sites in order to get food when they should be resting, or where they are housed in accommodation with appalling conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MOM look into providing guidelines on what constitutes adequate food and acceptable housing?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this will differ from employer to employer, we are not asking every employer to meet the standards in the same exact way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These guidelines will provide a minimum standard to ensure that employers cannot abuse the ambiguity of adequate food and acceptable housing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the Bill also proposes for the compensation to be assessed based on CI to expedite compensation for the employee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that, in practice, when the injury is assessed is important because employers consider their responsibilities to be fully discharged upon assessment of incapacity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can MOM clarify, where the assessment is based on CI, will the employer be responsible for the medical treatment after the assessment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, is the employer responsible for the cost of a follow-up treatment and for therapy after the assessment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify whether the Ministry’s intention is for migrant workers to be repatriated after assessment based on CI is done?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My concern is that this will have the effect of denying migrant workers continuing care and rehabilitation that may be necessary until their condition fully stabilises.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also proposed that employees be allowed to switch assessing doctors to address cases of inadequate care of overly conservative incapacity assessments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has stated that the Commissioner may allow employees to switch the assessing doctor in certain cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify under what circumstances the employee will be allowed to switch assessing doctors and whether the employee will be able to determine which doctor to consult?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the First Schedule of the Bill limits the compensation payable by an employer to the cost of medical treatment within one year of the date of the accident.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is plausible that bad employers may prevent or obstruct their employees from getting appropriate medical treatment in the first year after the accident.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In such cases, can the Ministry clarify whether the employee’s only recourse will be to seek compensation via the common law route?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I stand in support of what is an overall positive step in strengthening our work injury compensation regime.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My first concern, Mr Speaker, is that the Bill proposes to let insurance companies handle the processing of claims rather than it being under the purview of the Ministry for reasons of efficiency, as the Minister of State has alluded to.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate the intent but we will also agree that private insurers have no incentive to ensure workers are fully apprised of their rights and it is unclear which party is responsible for ascertaining validity and how a party can appeal the decision.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If it is to be private insurers making the decision, then there should be a rigorous Code of Practice or Conduct for them to follow to ensure integrity and reasonable speed in the process.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such a Code should include procedures and principles that align with the fundamental rules of natural justice, which include the principles of impartiality and fair hearing.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Arbiters must allow parties adequate opportunity to contest statements made by another party.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially important for workers, as employers may possess more documents and be able to withhold certain evidence more easily.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Migrant worker NGO, TWC2, has seen cases where the employer may under-declare overtime hours and, hence, salaries of migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He had filed WICA and salary claims at the same time.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, he was told to wait for his WICA claim to be completed before proceeding with his salary claim.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When the WICA compensation amount was offered nine months after the accident, it was based on the employer’s version of the AME.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, he accepted the compensation because he did not want to wait much longer and still had an outstanding salary claim.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, arbiters must be trained to scrutinise the evidence presented.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Under the Employment Act, employers are legally obliged to document working time records and pay slips and furnish these documents to the workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Adverse inference should be drawn against the employer who fails to keep or furnish proper records.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Recent amendments to the Employment Claims Act already mandate such inferences in salary claims.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It would also be useful to have the WICA and salary disputes to be conducted in parallel where there is a salary dispute, so that the AME can reflect the result of the salary claim process accurately.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, imperative that the Ministry implement safeguards to ensure that the insurers will process each claim in accordance with the worker's full rights and entitlements, including conducting spot checks on claims processed by insurers and monitoring the processing by insurers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is crucial since the insurer is paid for by the employers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, stringent external regulation is needed to ensure that the insurer acts impartially.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The changes in these procedures must be coupled with efforts to inform low-wage local and migrant workers of their insurance coverage and claims processes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Migrant workers, who rely on WICA for compensation, may be unable to push for their own interests if they lack a detailed understanding of the law.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Some workers mistakenly believe they have to bear their full medical expenses and avoid treatment, as they are not aware that it is mandated by law for employers to purchase WICA insurance.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, it is unclear how workers will receive information that a claim has been initiated by the employer.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Workers do not automatically receive accident reports from the Ministry when their accidents have been filed by their employer and, hence, may not see the details filed that may be prejudicial to the worker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While NGOs can email the Ministry on behalf of workers to request for a copy, the Ministry charges a fee for this.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the Ministry sends letters addressed to workers to the office address of the employer, but there have been cases where the employer has failed to pass these letters on to the workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider informing the workers immediately by short message service (SMS) and letting workers opt to obtain a free copy of the accident report and letters from a counter from the Ministry instead.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My second concern, Mr Speaker, is the delay in medical treatment or services received by migrant workers because of their employer’s refusal to pay, that essentially defeats the purpose of WICA, which is to ensure that workers are able to receive proper and, certainly, timely medical treatment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As we speak, a Bangladeshi worker, whom I will call Ahmad, is at risk of more damage from delayed treatment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Without the scans, the specialists are reluctant to determine further course of treatment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Other health professionals like physiotherapists also cannot help in the absence of diagnostic imaging.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Ahmad is currently supported by another NGO called HOME to get his employer to provide the undertaking and we are hoping he will be third time lucky to make the MRI appointment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A Chinese worker, whom I will call Liu, had an accident when he was hit in the eye by a large metal hook which caused a cornea rupture in his eye two months ago.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The doctor had indicated that he is mostly likely permanently blind in that eye.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, due to the lackadaisical approach to settling an outstanding bill of $200 by the employer, the Singapore National Eye Centre almost stopped Liu from seeing the specialist for follow-up which may have caused further damage.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Thankfully, HOME was able to support him through a kind donation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I do urge the Ministry to study the prevalence of this problem.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the proposed Code of Practice I mentioned earlier, insurers must also fulfil target timelines and settle the claims expeditiously, so that the medical treatment of workers are not delayed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill also provides that, upon the employer's insolvency, the insurer assumes "the same liabilities in relation to the employee as if the insurer were the employer." This suggests the insurer should pay for the medical treatment directly and not merely reimburse the worker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, clause 18 of the Bill provides that all compensation payable should be paid by the insurer to the injured worker or their representative if they are under incapacity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It would be helpful if the Minister could clarify whether the insurers will pay for the medical treatment directly, or reimburse the worker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, I would like to highlight the urgent need to safeguard the mental health of our migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A Bangladeshi worker, whom I will call Jamal, suffered work injuries in his hip and spine.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: His employer refused to pay for the total hip replacement he needed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He sought help with HealthServe, another NGO for migrant workers, which provided him shelter and supported him with his case to get the surgery he needed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In those six months with HealthServe, Jamal suffered great pain which caused insomnia and depressive moods that later escalated when he also met with a slew of major stressors, including his father having a stroke, his wife having left him and the loss of his home in Bangladesh due to flooding, and his escalating debts, and he thought of killing himself.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: HealthServe provided counselling to Jamal who reportedly cried several times during these sessions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He was repatriated in May 2019, broken in flesh and spirit.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider the following suggestions from the community.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, we must educate our migrant workers on mental health and provide peer support and/or mental health first aid training.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must provide easy access to counselling services for migrant workers in distress.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To my knowledge, there is only FASTCare by the Foreign Domestic Worker (FDW) Association for Social Support and Training by MOM for FDWs, but none yet for non-domestic and male migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am very happy to hear that HealthServe has plans to start a mental health programme but the needs are way more than what one NGO can handle.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, we could implement a structured intervention programme, such as a case management rehabilitation programme, which can improve several aspects of the workers’ psychological well-being and quality of life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This will provide the motivation to not only prepare injured workers to return to work but, more importantly, to help them adjust better and ensure sustainability in their post-rehabilitation work life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There is already successful implementation of such programmes in Malaysia and Germany.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, as I recall how heartening it was to see the different migrant communities coming together to support one another at the Migrant Cultural Show I was at last Sunday, I cannot help but think that we must surely include in that goal above, one that obliges us as a Government and society to enable and support our one million migrant brothers and sisters to be the best that they can be in total health and safety.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
