text: For if they help us build our homes and take care of much of our needs for us to thrive, how can we send them back to theirs, broken and less?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The coverage of the Act was in general extended to all workers, compensation limits were increased and processes were streamlined.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The cap for compensation on medical expenses was also raised.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In this Bill before the House, MOM has taken a more comprehensive approach.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed key changes cover four areas, namely, (a) enhanced protection of injured employees, (b) enhanced protection of employers' interests, (c) faster and simpler claims processes, and (d) increased deterrence against WICA contraventions.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is my belief that, especially in areas with potentially wide-ranging implications, such as those which this Bill touches on, it is the collective strength of our tripartite partnership that will engender the buy-in of all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, urge the Ministry to continue its efforts to engage the employers and, through the different labour unions, the employees, in constant dialogue.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In manifestation of this tripartite partnership, the Singapore National Employers' Federation, representing employers, has briefed and consulted 900 of our members on the proposed changes to WICA.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Several areas of concerns were raised from an employer's perspective.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: These concerns pertain largely to the proposed increase in the compensation limits and the likely corresponding increase in insurance premiums, the extension of compensation to employees on light duties, and the requirement to report any instance of work injury to MOM.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: While we, as employers, will continue to engage the Government through MOM, and our employees through our communications in the office and through the unions, please allow me now to share with this House the main inputs from employers alongside some of my own humble observations and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I will now address each of these in turn.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: First, all employees doing manual work, regardless of salary level, and all employees doing non-manual work, earning $1,600 or less a month, are currently required to be insured under WIC insurance bought by the employer.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: MOM has proposed raising this salary threshold to $2,600.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is heartening to note that MOM has proposed implementing this change in steps to give employers more time to adjust and re-evaluate their current WIC insurance plans.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, employers, at first sight, feel that the increase in coverage is too drastic as it will inevitably mean that companies will have to spend more in insurance premiums covering more employees.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Employees who are on light duties, are also proposed to be compensated.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: An employer who bought WIC insurance may not be able to claim compensation due to policy exclusions, for example, injury sustained from an accident which happened at a certain height.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, the proposed change to have the insurers offering a standard WIC insurance policy, helps to prevent disputes and provides more certainty to employers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With the change, the licensed insurers will take over MOM's claim processing role.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The standard insurance coverage and the taking over of the claims process by the insurance companies, together with the higher compensation limits, point to a potential increase in insurance premiums.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Is the Ministry also able to provide clarity on what is the expected increase in premium for a business?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Employers will need to factor this increase into their total business cost.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially important, in the context of today's challenging business climate and this information will go some way towards assisting us to assuage the fears of employers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Another avenue which is likely to lead to increased costs for businesses is the requirement for employers to report to MOM for all instances of work-related injuries, including light duty incidents.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This will increase administrative work and compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Employers hope that MOM will look into how to operationalise this efficiently and perhaps offer financial incentives for employers with a clean record.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The next aspect I would like to touch on in my speech is a call for better outreach and education to businesses for compensation for employees on light duty due to work-related injury.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Employees who are injured due to work-related accidents are compensated based on AME for the first 14 days of outpatient sick leave or 60 days of hospitalisation leave, and two-thirds AME thereafter, up to one year.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: With the proposed extension of WIC to employees on light duties, the concept of AME will also apply to this group of injured employees.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I hope MOM will engage businesses better to educate employers who have trouble in understanding or operationalising this new requirement.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: One commonly asked question would be how this requirement would apply to an employee who is on light duty but fails to report for work with valid reasons.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: One of the proposed changes under this Bill relates to the licensing regime for insurers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: WIC insurance premiums currently range from around 0.3% to 1.5% of wages.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This, in my opinion, is a step forward for the WIC insurance market, taking after the current practice in the motor insurance market.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This differentiation would necessarily influence employers who are "not so safe" now, to reduce their exposure to workplace injury risks. "Safe" employers will be motivated to continue to maintain their high level of WSH standard.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This is also one of the strategies laid out under "Strengthening WSH Ownership" in the WSH2028 report, released in April this year.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: That being said, with this requirement, MOM will now be yet another repository of information.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: It is important, therefore, that access to such information must be safeguarded and employers should be informed what information could be shared with insurers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to this, I would like to suggest to the insurers to introduce a preferential rate or incentive scheme, similar to the no-claim bonus concept in the motor insurance market.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This would now be viable, with the sharing of past claim data with the insurers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This would provide employers an incentive to place greater emphasis on WSH.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This would be a win-win-win situation for the employees, employers and insurers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill plays an important part towards our journey to make Singapore amongst the world's best in WSH.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: That includes their health and safety at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should provide a safe work environment and employees should do their part and follow safety practices I affirm my support for the Bill but, at the same time, reiterate the legitimate concerns that the employers have.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that MOM will address these concerns and lend enhanced support to employers.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As a firm advocate for the tripartite arrangement, I strongly believe that, with the Government's support, both employees and employers can help Singapore achieve sooner the WSH2028 vision of A Healthy Workforce in Safe Workplaces; A Country Renowned for Best Practices in Workplace Safety and Health.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Self-employed persons in this context are typically defined as workers for their own account.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The idea is that in some very important sense, self-employed persons as independent contractors can better take care of themselves and their work.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This is a fundamental and long-standing distinction traceable to the English common law, and for good reason.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The bargaining powers of the contracting parties are often unequal.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Let us continue to study how these more vulnerable workers for their own account are differently situated in meaningful ways from others employed under, say, a part-time or short-term contract of service.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Do these differences really represent a greater ability on the part of the workers to take care of themselves and their work that warrant the contractors/employers doing significantly less for them?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: How many hours of work and at what time of day or week are in effect readily available for the worker to choose from, and on what notice?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While we push for safety first at zero accidents, workplace injuries do happen.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments to better regulate insurance coverage with limited exclusions provide clarity as insurers cannot include non-approved exclusions.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Also, the proposed appeals channel by MOM for workers who dispute claims as assessed by insurers is much welcomed as it provides recourse for the injured workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, the measures to encourage better safety track records of the companies based on differentiated insurance premium, the employer's risk profile and claim history will give greater impetus for employers to partner unions in ensuring a safe, healthy workplace for all workers which I will address later in my speech.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While these proposed amendments are most welcomed, I would like to see clarity on three issues and put forth some suggestions.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The first is the WIC due to the nature of work arrangements and insurance coverage.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As flexible work arrangements become increasingly adopted by employers, such as working from home or telecommuting, will WICA cover any work injuries sustained during work outside of the workplace, specifically when work accidents occur when the worker is on flexi-work from home?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As automation and technology increasingly change the way we work, we are seeing more working people multitasking, taking up additional job roles and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: While they might be considered as non-manual workers, part of their job responsibilities will increasingly expand.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Their day-to-day job might be office-based but the job roles and functions might require them to be around in an environment where the risk of injury is high.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These employees might be drawing a salary beyond the stated amount of $2,600.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: So, may I suggest that more be done to encourage employers to buy insurance coverage for all employees?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Correct me if I am wrong, but the answer is none.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: With the increasing prevalence of contract for service and the gig economy, they will not fall under the ambit of WICA as service buyers who engage them will not have to take up a WICA-related insurance coverage for these self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: What recourse do these employees then have in the event of injuries sustained in the course of their employment?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), through the Tripartite Standards on Procurement of Service from media freelancers, provided details on insurance coverage for media freelancers to be covered by their companies if they are required to offer their service onsite or on locations specified by the companies.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The work-related personal accident insurance covers against claims for death, total permanent disability and medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As such, the responsibility is on the freelancers to ensure that they are insured with personal accident insurance that will be paid by the buyer while the service buyers should be prepared to factor such insurance cost into their service fee.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Will other Government Procurement Entities (GPEs) consider taking the lead to provide work injury insurance, especially for a significant GPE like MOE's schools, as this will help set the tone and shape responsible procurement practices where work injury insurance is the norm for responsible outsourcing?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As a unionist, I have come across members who have been diagnosed with depression.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: One such member initially wanted to resign from the company when diagnosed with depression.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: But the company persuaded him not to do so and to continue his employment while undergoing treatment.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: He was granted sick leave for a year with medical review done every month.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: During this period, the company paid his basic salary and medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: After more than a year of therapy and medication, there was no improvement to the member's condition.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The company had to reluctantly terminate his employment.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: This member was fortunate as the company continued to pay his salary and medical treatment for a year, but what happens if an employer opts to terminate an employee with mental illness at the early onset of the condition?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Can WICA be extended to cover the medical expenses and wages for such illnesses?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: After all, mental wellness is an area not very much talked about, but it is an increasing trend in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: On the amendment to provide for a differentiated WICA insurance premium based on the employer's risk profile and claims history, it now gives more significant incentives to companies to ensure a safe and healthy workplace for its employees.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Here, the companies can partner the union to develop a safe and healthy culture in the company.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: One such example is PSA, the port operator.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The Port's unions have a close partnership in working with PSA to raise safety standards at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Unions and management have worked closely together to improve workers' training and implement work procedures to create a safe work environment.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: To assimilate HSSE in the work culture, PSA has also developed an inhouse workshop programme called "Starfish".

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Union leaders are part of the first batch trained alongside PSA leaders and we have provided feedback to strengthen the course structure and material for the subsequent rollout to all our workers.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Union leaders also play a vital role in rallying workers' support for safety-related initiatives.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These collective efforts have resulted in significant improvements in safety standards in PSA over the years and have helped in the reduction of costs.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: An injury is one too many, and we are partnering management to cultivate a generative safety culture.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: The Labour Movement aims to create a safe and conducive environment for every worker in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: We also call on our companies to work with the unions to promote safety and health at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: As union leaders, we can and will be the ambassadors and catalysts at the workplace to promote health and safety at the workplace.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is an improvement from our current system, reducing time spent on paperwork by all parties, particularly the victims and their families, during a very stressful and difficult time.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would just like to seek clarification on instances when claims assessment on injuries are delayed because employers are slow in paying for or guaranteeing the necessary medical examinations.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, they or the insurance companies pay for clinic visits or hospital stays but not necessarily for outpatient tests, such as scans.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on any changes or improvements, if any, for such cases that are provided for in this Bill?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I have a question regarding the proposal to compensate employees placed on light duties due to work injuries.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The intention of the Ministry is that these workers should not be worse off than those who are given medical leave.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, injured employees on medical leave are compensated with their AME.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under this Bill, compensation will be equal for both, but I would like to ask if there are definitions of what injuries can be addressed with light duties versus medical leave.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, I would like to seek clarification on surveillance on reporting by employers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There may still be employers who do not report smaller injuries.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What measures are in place to minimise this problem?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employees are required under WICA to inform their employers of any incidents as soon as possible.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there a way whereby the employee reporting process informs both their employers and MOM simultaneously, possibly through a one-step reporting system at the health professionals' office for greater efficiency?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such a system will also ensure that employers do not have the opportunity to under-report.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I noticed that a key difference is that a number of these countries offer the option of pensions for workers who suffer permanent disabilities.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Here, in Singapore, workers can only claim a lump sum.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fixed amounts offer certainty for employers and insurers but may impose greater hardship on employers as we live longer.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The disbursement of such a large sum of money all at once has the risks that it may all be spent too quickly or unwisely.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, in the Federal Republic of Germany, under the statutory occupational accident insurance, such workers receive a pension until the age of 65, unless he or she begins receiving old-age pension earlier than that age.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They can also opt for the pension to be paid out as a lump sum.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Furthermore, in the event of death, any children they have who are under 18 years of age will receive an orphan's pension.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similarly, in Western Australia, in addition to a lump-sum payment capped at AUD$232,000, there is a provision for a periodic child's allowance for dependent children.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the United Kingdom, on top of compensation from the compulsory Employers' Liability insurance bought by companies, affected employees can receive between £35.80 and £179 weekly under the Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit scheme, depending on the level of disablement.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the US, there is no federal oversight nor minimum standard.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every state has its own workers compensation system and they vary widely.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Overall, the proposed amendments will essentially make the Bill more worker-centric.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For many low-wage workers, a sizeable portion of their pay package comprises overtime payments, allowances and incentive payments while doing their regular work.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More importantly, it also prevents the occurrence of possible abuse of the system where the injured vulnerable worker may be given medical leave for less than the stipulated four days as a way to get around the duty to report for WICA and the remaining recovery period is covered by light duties.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such circumventing measures may arise as company-approved medical practitioners may face the dilemma of balancing their financial interest against their ethical obligation when it comes to prescribing appropriate duration of medical leave for the workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Employment Act has been amended to make it mandatory for employers to issue pay slips.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will benefit the low-wage and migrant worker sectors where the absence of pay slips tend to be more prevalent.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, this makes WICA to be more worker-centric and responsive to the specific needs and situations for the migrant workers as it levels the playing ground for migrant worker claimants and evens up the odds in favour of workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: MWC had encountered cases involving injured foreign workers who were required to stay in Singapore for extended claims, but not allowed to work and, inevitably, run into difficulty with upkeeping and maintaining themselves.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are good reasons to suspect that some employers or insurers may deliberately drag the cases because they are aware the migrant worker will run into hardship and put the employers or insurers at an advantage to negotiate a lower quantum which the worker has little choice but to accept, or even hold out on payment, against which the worker has no means, whether in terms of time or money, to enforce.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, all employers are required to have Compulsory Medical Insurance for their migrant workers but, most employers will only ensure minimum medical insurance coverage for their migrant workers to meet MOM's requirement.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our laws require the employers to be liable for the medical treatment for the foreign workers, some employers will incur huge medical expenses for their injured migrant workers if the WICA cases drag on for too long, since all foreigners are charged unsubsidised rates for treatment and hospital stay.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, the increased WICA coverage for treatment, together with expedited claims payouts will certainly help in cases where urgent medical treatment is needed by the worker but, the employer is unable to pay due to lack of medical insurance coverage or other cost issues.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another issue arising from claims processing times is the situation where employers do not provide accommodation or maintenance for their claimant workers anymore or the worker himself wishes to leave his employer's hold, given the breakdown in their relationship for whatever reasons.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The migrant workers who decide to stay on pending the outcome of their injury claims are generally prohibited from working, which may cause them a lot of financial hardship.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A situation where the injured migrant workers opt to stay on their own and are unable to work legally to support their own maintenance and upkeep is undesirable, given the potential for them to moonlight illegally which will deny them all the employment protections.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some may succumb to anti-social or even criminal behaviour in a bid to survive, which is detrimental to our society's well-being and safety.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thus, expediting the claims processing time will minimise the cost of their maintenance and upkeep and perhaps, lessen the likelihood of the migrant workers facing financial hardship and having to resort to undesirable actions that would be detrimental to themselves and our society.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the changes made to WICA, there is a need to raise workers' awareness through outreach efforts, especially among the vulnerable low-wage and migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many vulnerable workers are still unaware of the basic provisions under WICA, like how you can still claim under common law even after filing for WICA, but cannot do so in the reverse.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some injured vulnerable workers may file injury claim under common law at the advice of overzealous lawyers without realising that they are signing away their rights to a WICA claim.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They might also be unaware how WICA differs from legal suits under common law in its compensation quantum and other aspects like standards of proof and others.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There must also be concerted efforts to change the mindset of employers to see WICA as an extension of the company's Work-Safety-Health worksite culture where employers are themselves briefed extensively in WSH and WICA laws and these aspects are refreshed regularly in worksite safety briefings and meetings.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such efforts will result in a general levelling up of the understanding of WSH and WICA for both employers and their workers, thus minimising potential cause for misunderstanding and disputes.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ideally, such established channels must be guided by MOM and not by employers or insurance companies who might make it too onerous for workers seeking reassessment.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some occupational diseases (ODs) can be undiagnosed for a prolonged period.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can workers be compensated for such work-related injuries or diseases?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our Government is also encouraging older workers to work, would the standard WICA insurance clauses be inclusive to ensure employers can buy insurance coverage for all their workers?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since older workers are sometimes prone to injuries due to slips and falls, some insurance companies may have exclusion clauses, in fine print, to exclude coverage for older workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will lead to more expeditious claims processing but, with check and balances by MOM to ensure fairness to all parties.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the past, MOM processed the claims and was perceived to be the guardian of fairness of the WICA claim.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, outsourcing this function to MOM-licensed insurers may lead to the judgement being questioned in terms of fairness as the insurance companies have a vested interest to keep compensation on the low side.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, insurance companies may also try to keep premiums low for their policies to be competitive but, at the expense of being able to have sufficient financial standing to give our workers adequate and fair compensation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To mitigate this, NTUC welcomes the system of controls and penalties to accompany this legal innovation to ensure insurers remain on-side, fair and objective in their assessment.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How effective this new licensing and enforcement regime will be can only be reassessed after the new system has been in place for some time.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the meantime, the unions and MWC will continue to get a better ground-sensing when we help our workers in their claims under WICA.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nevertheless, we urge the policymakers to review the application of the new insurer-processed system at appropriate junctures, so that further review and strengthening may continue to be made to it along the way to more effectively safeguard the rights and welfare of the key intended beneficiaries of the Act.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   NTUC supports the amendments to WICA because it will provide better protection to workers who suffer injuries while working.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, the amendments also ensure a more stable insurance coverage with limited exclusions, which ensures that employers and workers can submit appeals to receive compensation for most types of injuries that commonly happen to workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although the responsibility for processing appeals for compensation under this Act is given to insurers appointed by MOM, these amendments will still allow workers to challenge the compensation amount that is given, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For employers, these amendments also help to reduce the cost of buying WICA insurance which will become more affordable provided they have a good safety record, whereby not many of their workers suffer injuries while working.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: WICA is a very useful Act for workers, but it is important that the Ministry take steps to enhance workers' awareness towards this Act, especially for low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will prevent irresponsible employers from taking advantage by cheating injured workers so that the workers do not submit appeals to obtain compensation through WICA, which affects the company's accident record.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): I believe that we are, indeed, making a big step in the right direction for our workers here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The proposed amendments show that we understand the urgency of workplace compensations and the need to be fair and transparent to all parties involved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At this juncture, I also want to declare my interest as I work for an organisation that handles work injury assessments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Employers have a duty of care to provide a safe environment for those who work for them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: WICA's "no-fault system" ensures that employees receive fair compensation for work-related injuries or illnesses without having to go through the lengthy and costly process of taking legal action against their employer.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Both workplace major and minor injuries saw an increase in the number of cases.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed enhancements to compensation to keep pace with healthcare cost and wage growth and the amendments to make it compulsory for employers to take WIC insurance coverage for employees will provide assurance to employees of fair compensation and ensures timely payout of compensation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed amendments to make all MCs and light duties reportable and expansion of compensation to cover workers on light duties due to work injury will be key to preventing employers from influencing doctors on the prescription of MCs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This ensures that workers are given appropriate number of days of MCs for their recovery and care.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With employers having to take compulsory insurance coverage for WIC, we must, however, be cognisant that this will have increased cost impact on businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clause 24 states that the insurance policies must be approved policies with one or more designated insurers and that a minimum coverage may be stipulated.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clause 26 requires that an approved policy must contain all the prescribed compulsory terms and disallows derogatory of the compulsory terms.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Clause 25 outlines the penalties for employers who breach the terms set out in clause 24 which include fines, imprisonment or both.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With such obligations placed on employers, what measures will there be to ensure insurance premiums for work insurance compensation remain affordable and sustainable for businesses, especially given the current market challenges that businesses are facing?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I was glad that Minister of State stated that there will be a phased approach taken in the implementation of the amendments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But despite this, because of increased scope of compensation that will come with the amendments as well as the fact that more employees will be required to be covered under this Act, it will definitely increase the cost of premiums.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I do hope that there will be measures to also look at the premium affordability and the trends of how that posed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed new regulatory regime for Workplace Insurance Compensation does, however, offer better protection for employers as well as only insurers licensed by MOM are allowed to sell the approved WIC policies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: MOM's endorsement of a standard WIC policy with a core set of insurance terms and conditions will also help ensure claims are paid and employers will not be faced with exclusions and have to make out-of-pocket payment of compensation to employees despite having insurance coverage.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The regime will also require licensed insurers to process all WIC claims in accordance with stipulated terms and conditions, guidelines as well as processing timelines.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, in the event of disputes, this will be reviewed and handled by MOM.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, this does provide additional protection for employers directly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Under the current Act as well, employers have no recourse against fraudulent claims if they have made payment for medical, permanent incapacity or death compensation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As outlined in clause 33 of the Bill, insurers will also be required to provide MOM with policy and claims history information.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This information will be centralised and, I believe, shared with insurers to allow insurers to differentiate premiums based on claims history and the risk profile of employers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This concept is a novel idea and may encourage employers to ensure safe and healthy workplaces.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, the devil is always in the details and the exact implementation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, can MOM share more information on how this will work?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Will there will be greater transparency on the differentiation of premiums and will employers also be provided with information of the insurance premium trends to allow them to also make better decisions on the insurers that they select?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would also ask that MOM consider the approach of sharing of information of good work safety practices of employers and having this included as part of premium differentiation because this will help also prevent a practice of under-reporting because if the claims history was the way of premium differentiation, it could lead to a dangerous situation of under-reporting.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the proposal for new and enhanced penalties to deter employers from non-compliance, I do also ask how MOM will keep track of compliance to ensure that employers do, in fact, take up WIC insurance coverage for their employees and reporting of all work injuries and illnesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the same time, will there also be tracking of the adequacy as well as the timeliness of payouts by insurers to ensure that employees do get paid appropriately as well as in a timely manner?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I see the purpose of regulations covering workplace safety as addressing two problems: first, the imbalance of power between the worker and the employer; and second, the market failures inherent in the provision of workplace safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, quite apart from the question of justice, there are economic efficiencies to be gained from good regulations covering workplace safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While no employer intends for workplace injuries to occur, employers face incentives to minimise expenditures on safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While the common law provides for redress, the legal system is costly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, WICA is really a means of ensuring that the employers internalise the costs of injuries at work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Employers have to pay the correct price for any deficiencies in workplace safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Without WICA, it is clear that the costs of work injury are more likely to fall on the worker and the family and, in extremis, society as taxpayers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This provides a market-based mechanism for improving workplace safety efficiently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the mechanism could function even better if the employer's risk-loading was publicly reported so that workers and other firms can make decisions, bearing the employer's safety record in mind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, even if we welcome these improvements to workplace safety, we should examine two related problems of workplace safety which face continuing market failures – the case of self-employed persons and the insurance and medical ecosystem that give WICA effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The first concerns self-employed persons, particularly those providing services through market platforms – our private hire drivers, taxi drivers, food delivery riders and the like.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In principle, this is because self-employed persons are not subject to the control of an employer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We expect that the self-employed are best placed to judge the risks of a particular task and how to mitigate those risks efficiently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But in practice, the risks faced by the self-employed are really no different from those faced by the employee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Traffic accidents, slips and falls do not check for whether you are employed or self-employed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are now competing employment arrangements in the market for point-to-point drivers and food delivery riders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At least one taxi company engages drivers as employees rather than as self-employed hirers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Food delivery services also employ some delivery riders directly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A market platform that chooses to employ workers directly will have to comply with WICA and pay the appropriate insurance costs for the risks, in addition to bearing other regulatory costs of employment, such as Central Provident Fund contributions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, because the regulatory costs are, in effect, shared between employer and the employed, it means that take-home wages for the self-employed may well be higher than that for employees, for the same type of task.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While the self-employed may see this as a good thing, the self-employed are really going to be underpriced in the market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Their wages will not reflect the full risks of the job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The self-employed and their families will end up bearing the real costs if they suffer injuries in the course of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge that there are Government efforts to promote work injury insurance for the self-employed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Private Accident Insurance will not be subject to specific regulation under WICA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we have no regulatory levers for ensuring that the comprehensiveness of coverage, standards for claims and processes for payment are similar to the protections provided under WICA, or even if they are adequate for risks of the task.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One objection to regulating self-employed persons for work injuries is the cost burden.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Who will pay for the costs and how will protection be organised?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I believe the market platforms have a role to play.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The market platforms already handle payments between self-employed persons and the buyers of their services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The platforms have the necessary economies of scale to contract with insurers to provide coverage for their drivers and riders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While this is currently voluntary, we should study whether it is possible to improve workplace injury protection for self-employed persons on market platforms to the same standard as that enjoyed by employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The second area where we need to understand market failures in safety better is the broader safety ecosystem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are two other parties playing a major role in WICA: the insurers, who guarantee the payment of liabilities under WICA, and the medical institutions, who treat the injured and provide medical reports for the purpose of computing compensation under WICA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is that both insurers and medical institutions face significant conflicts of interest in discharging their roles under WICA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While insurers should, in principle, price insurance premiums appropriately so that the employer bears the eventual cost of lapses in safety, the insurers also have an incentive to reduce payouts to the extent possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While the move to have WICA insurers process all claims is administratively efficient, I urge the Ministry to continue monitoring the performance of insurers in claims processing, with the interests of the injured worker in mind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, I urge the Ministry to commit to sampling and independently assessing claims, to determine if injured workers are receiving their full entitlements under WICA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As for medical institutions, the concern here is that the medical providers effectively work for the employer and not the injured patient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many employers have established contracts with medical providers for employment-related medical services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is when medical providers face a conflict of interest between their duty to the patient and their financial relationship to the employer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While I acknowledge that the Ministry is monitoring this issue closely, there are some regulatory reforms that could grant workers more protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To guard against the inefficient inflation of claims, the Ministry could establish a set of medical institutions that are approved for this purpose, such as the restructured hospitals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I trust that the Ministry will continue to work with the market platforms to provide full and equivalent protection for self-employed Singaporeans, and with NGOs to support migrant workers in their pursuit of justice.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I manage some of these work-related injuries and deaths at work and I also write their assessment and compensation claims.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Pertaining to the technical aspects of the Bill, I have the following queries.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is the trend that we are seeing over the last few years?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is a reflection of our workplace safety.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, how does it compare with other cities with relatively similar industrial and size make-up as Singapore?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can we not just do this in one step?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For such an important issue whereby lives and limbs can be at stake, the faster the better.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister explain this in a bit more detail and how the decision was reached to do this in two steps rather than just one step?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thirdly, there may be cases where the salary records are missing or unavailable.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I note one of the prerequisites is the itemised payslip.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How can we reconcile and improve this as it seems a fundamental and basic requirement for employers?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Is there a significant number of such cases that MOM faces annually?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How can we perhaps implement some kind of enforcement with this because this is really a basic fundamental for our workers?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourth, for some cases where their medical status needs stabilisation before the final compensation can be decided upon, they will need multiple follow-ups and appointments with the medical specialists.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, who will pay for these consultation fees?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are these claimable from the employers or MOM?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, these follow-ups are done before the claims are given out.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, the workers will usually have to fork out their own money for this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These fees may amount to quite a significant value and, at times, the employees have no choice but to follow up.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In some cases, we have also seen them defaulting on their follow-up, thus leading to problems medically for them.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister also share with us on the claims for dental procedures and dental cases that are related to injuries?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are employees only able to attend Government or public dental services or can private dental specialist care also be recognised as well, as dental injuries are probably less common than just medically-related ones?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One other area which is still rather nebulous is the area of mental incapacitation resulting from a work-related issue.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One of our colleagues Mr Arasu Duraisamy brought this up earlier and I support his call for some considerations in this area.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, has there been any examples of such cases, if the Minister can share with us?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, moving forward, how can we perhaps give these cases some kind of consideration?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Next, claims from workers can be reported by the workers, employers or the medical practitioners.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: That would be good for us to understand as well.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, perhaps some expedition in this area will be useful.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to statistics from MOM, the number of workplace injury cases is rising.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The statistics showed also that although fatal injury cases had decreased, the number of major and minor workplace injury cases saw an increase.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed amendments to WICA are, therefore, timely as it seeks to provide a faster and better way to compensate employees in the event of an unfortunate accident occurring at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the past year, I have been advocating for differentiated WIC insurance premiums, based on companies’ risk profiles and claims records.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am, therefore, glad to see that this suggestion has been adopted.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Differentiated insurance premiums will incentivise companies with strong workplace safety practices to continue their focus on creating a safe working environment and encourage companies with poor track records to improve their workplace safety practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nudging companies to focus on their workplace safety culture is important as this will directly result in a better safety outcome for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Labour Movement has also worked closely with MOM on other key measures in the Bill that will result in enhanced protection for employees.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These include expanding the coverage of compulsory WIC insurance to more employees and extending WIC to include employees on light duty who may be paid significantly less than usual due to their work injury but are not eligible for medical leave.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such measures will, undoubtedly, enhance the protection of employees in the area of workplace safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we also need to look at WSH holistically by placing equal emphasis on workplace health, which is the latter – and often overlooked – half of the WSH equation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have some suggestions on how we can do exactly that.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our workplaces are becoming increasingly desk-bound, particularly for many of our PMEs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Studies have shown that sedentary jobs give rise to new forms of occupational diseases, many of which are not covered under WICA.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, long working hours, coupled with a stressful workplace environment, can result in mental health issues, such as workplace burnout, which is now a recognised occupational phenomenon by the World Health Organization. "Feeling burnout" is a common phrase we hear from our workers, among our workers, but little has been done to learn more about its longer-term health issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such occupation-related mental health issues can lead and have led to negative physical health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we are not ready to do so, we should at least initiate more studies on the effects of such workplace work-related mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can quip about how to label such mental health issues, whether it is an occupational phenomenon or a work-related disease.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is clear, however, is that we need to protect our workers who may be suffering in silence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For WSH to be pervasive in every industry, companies must also embrace Total WSH and encourage their employees to lead a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, those companies with staff canteens can provide healthier food options for their workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The canteens operated by the National Transport Workers Union (NTWU) have done exactly this through our Brown Rice campaign, which has been a big success across our 46 canteens island-wide.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have also tried to promote sugar-free drinks, such as Kopi-O kosong and Teh-O kosong.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, this has not been as successful as the brown rice initiative, but we will try again.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through constant experimentation, I believe that we will be able to find the right initiatives to encourage healthy eating among our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What we eat is key to what we turn out to be.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to partner companies to introduce more initiatives to promote healthy eating and achieve Total WSH.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a good idea and we need to ensure that there are sufficient safeguards in place.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Insurers may have vested interest in reducing the number of work injury claims to reduce the compensation that is paid out.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, it is vital that MOM set up channels for workers to seek redress if they disagree with the insurer’s assessment on the validity of their claims.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Beyond MOM's proposed role as adjudicator of any WIC disputes, MOM should also have levers to penalise insurers who indiscriminately dismiss claims as non-work injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under the proposed licensing regime, MOM will accredit WIC policies based on a core set of standard terms and conditions to ensure adequate WIC insurance coverage.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, insurers would still be permitted to offer exclusion clauses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As I have mentioned earlier, 2018 saw a total of 12,810 workplace accidents reported across all industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every accident that happens, even the minor ones, is a danger to our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Inherent in every injury is the risk that it may worsen and result in a tragedy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Seemingly minor injuries at the first instance can worsen into a major injury and a major injury can lead to death.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Here, I would like to reiterate the calls that I have made on how we can step up on prevention, as well as provide MOM with a suggestion on how to use the data from the WIC claims to help in conducting targeted inspections and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a mandatory WSH representative in every company will certainly go a long way in making Total WSH more pervasive and help prevent accidents from happening.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Ministry can reconsider this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Centre can establish a central registry of WSH practitioners, share industry best practices and showcase the use of new technologies to strengthen safety and health standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) would be the greatest beneficiaries of such a Centre of Excellence, as they have limited resources and would benefit from such knowledge sharing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we put the pieces of the new legislative framework in place, we need to be mindful that WSH needs to be tackled holistically.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Only by focusing equally on preventing workplace accidents and on Workplace Health initiatives can we truly achieve Total WSH.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first pertains to his remarks or the allusion that this is a subject that the Workers' Party has suddenly developed some sort of interest in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have most of the Parliamentary Questions that were filed by Members on WIC for this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not going to make the argument that the Members of Parliament who did not file any questions have no interest in WICA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Having said that, the Minister of State also said that the Workers' Party Members of Parliament – and correct me if I am wrong – did not ask any question on it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I believe in 2017, there was a question filed and – I mean, not filed, sorry – a question filed by Members and Ms Sylvia Lim had supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I believe in his reply, the Minister of State said that it was rejected because it was out of time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But in the letter that was sent to R, the Commissioner of Labour stated that – and I will read out the paragraph, it is a short one – "We understand that you met the accident before you reached the training venue." That is the first reason and the second is, "You did not make a compensation claim under WICA within one year from the date of the accident." So, my question is: the first reason, it is settled law that if you are injured on your way to work from your workplace, that you can claim under WICA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I am not sure why that statement was made to R.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I suggested in my speech that it could be because of the way R framed his claim, in the first instance, to MOM.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, can the Minister of State just confirm that?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The third issue is a question I asked in my speech which was to give the House a sense of the numbers of all successful WICA claims by foreign and local workers over the last five years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not believe the Minister of State answered that question and the breakdown of workers who chose a Common Law remedy, private compensation and those who did not proceed with their claims respectively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The final query I have, which was also in my speech, was about whether MOM follows up with private compensations, whether MOM inquires with employer, whether MOM takes a proactive view as to whether that compensation is fair vis-a-vis WICA.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the first point on the Parliamentary Questions (PQs), yes, we checked by PQs filed, so I mentioned that there were no PQs filed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To me, what is more important is that we are all here, like I said, it is never too late to start.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One was it was after more than one year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The second one, if the Member notice, after we admitted the case, we agreed that it was indeed one that WICA can cover or WICA should cover.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, in my earlier speech, I did mention that both employer and employee did not think it was a WICA case or it was a work-related case.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, therefore, as a result, I do not think anyone thought – whether the employer or the worker – none of them felt it was work-related injury.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: After the case was admitted, we were then able to look deeper into the case and interviewed both employer and employee to understand why it was that way.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, at the end of the day, the employee still got the case done and it was treated as WICA.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the statistics that were asked for, I do not think this is the right platform to provide that.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is better that the Member files a PQ to get the statistics.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have it but we have to prepare it for the Member in the way he has asked for it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was about whether MOM tracks private settlements and whether they are fair for the worker.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, therefore, it will be more meaningful for us to use the database, moving forward with the new WICA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick follow-up again on the first point about R's case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I understand the employer and the worker both did not believe that this was a legitimate claim under WICA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My point is that the Commissioner of Labour also felt that way at the first instance; and my concern is the law is quite settled on this issue and it is surprising that at the first instance, it was not picked up at the MOM level.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Like I said, there were two trigger points.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First was, I suppose, beyond one year, the case was not able to be admitted, to begin with.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, therefore, at that point in time, it was not possible to determine the facts of the case and to determine whether truly or not the accounts were valid and the views were valid.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It was only after the fact, when MOM had spoken to both employer and employee, were they able to establish that both of them did not think it was a work injury case.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It would not have been practical to have just assumed, at face value, until you go deeper into investigations and of which after investigations and after we admitted the appeal, we understood the case better and, therefore, we admitted the case and awarded it accordingly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think in this case the employee had also made the application two years after the incident and after leaving the firm so, therefore, at face value, it had breached the one-year liability by the employer.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, to that extent, it was rejected upfront.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: After appeals – and this is what we do – on appeal, we reviewed the case, we investigated deeper.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And, therefore, upon investigation, we found that both of them did not think it was but, after clarifications, we took the case in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a last point, Mr Speaker, I do not want to belabour the point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The point I am making is: this is a worker who has received the letter from MOM.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If he had not gone for an additional recourse, seen his Member of Parliament, he could have well said, "Look, MOM has rejected me as being out of time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Number two, they are telling me that I cannot claim because it is not claimable under WICA since I wasn't injured in the workplace", confirming his own state of mind that actually this is not an injury he can claim for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What I am saying is: if you put yourself in the shoes of the worker, you would realise that actually the answer MOM gave was wrong.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Not the one-year timebar, but the point about it not being a claimable injury.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that is the issue which I am a bit concerned about.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I do not have the letter with me.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But, like I said, there were two triggers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, hopefully, in future, we will have better visibility on such appeals and the process to facilitate it.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I think there should be no exclusion clauses, especially in fine print, to deny any age group because it will affect their employability.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Can I have that assurance that all age groups will be covered?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Well, we have not reached the part where we define the terms for this insurance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But, certainly, we will study it and take it on board and take the Member's suggestions on board.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: I agree with the Minister of State that the problem is service buyers lack the economy of scale to provide WIC coverage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: But the Government is a large service buyer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: So, could the Government consider leading the way when buying services from self-employed persons to provide WIC-equivalent coverage, much as you are already going to be doing for contribute-as-you-earn in the future?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The relationship, as I mentioned, between self-employed persons and employers are very different.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers set the conditions in which you work and, therefore, you deal with WICA in this case.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is a lot more certainty in the environments that you are dealing with.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For self-employed persons, as I mentioned, the self-employed person serves multiple buyers, not just the Government but someone else.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it is difficult to manage in that sense.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But having said that, we will continue to encourage them to undertake both PAI as well as PML.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think that is the logical thing to do and, perhaps, that will be priced in, hopefully, as how they charge for their service.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have seen, as I mentioned, the major players coming on board and we will encourage others to do so and continue the effort.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The first is on the Code of Practice or Code of Conduct for the insurance companies that I mentioned in the speech.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The Minister of State had assured us that he will make sure that the insurers would treat each claim fairly and in a timely manner.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Can the Minister of State share with us how he would do that because these are private companies?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: He cited that there were three claims on psychological illness in the period cited.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I shared that there were 60% of migrant workers that are predicted to have serious mental illness.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: So, that disconnect with the number of claims that had been made – the three cases versus the 60% – I wonder if that is a case of both the employers and the employees, especially the employees, are not aware that they can actually make the claim.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: This comes from my own personal interaction with two Bangladeshi workers whom I supported because they were under such extreme distress and not knowing that they can actually claim for this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Without that link, it is not possible to cover it under this Act.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In a certain sense, you cannot sell WICA insurance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you want to get into this business, you have to abide by the regulations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, that is the ultimate assurance that we can give employers, in terms of the terms that the WICA insurers set.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There are certain terms we need them to cover and these will be covered.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, the database for the insurers as well, there is assurance that employers do not under-insure.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, the whole scheme of things works by providing more transparency for both the employer, the insurer as well as the worker.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is a certain sense that the assurance is being provided to create a different ecosystem that is based on greater transparency.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: So, the Minister of State is saying that mental illness resulting from a work injury is covered.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Is that explicitly stated so that employees are aware and also the NGOs and the medical institutions?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I said work accident and injury resulting from an accident.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it has to be a mental health condition, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), resulting from an accident.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: But is it explicitly stated or is it implied?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister of State give an example of a mental illness as a result of work accident that is claimable under WICA?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They suffered PTSD after an accident that they faced.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Apart from this physical injury, they also had mental injury as a result.      .
